item.title: Open Source Summit + Embedded Linux Conference Europe 2026 (Prague) report and presentation notes
item.description:
Finally I sufficiently edited my notes for a little belated post on the Open Source Summit + Embedded Linux Conference Europe 2026 in Prague. I was quite excited to attend as it was my first conference/summit, and it certainly delivered. Organizationally, it was handled very well, and there were always plenty of presentations, booths, and activities to attend. The schedule was also planned in such a way that coming up to the booths to talk about projects (which ranged from things like Flatcar container Linux to RISC-V automotive projects and many, many more across the entire open source and embedded space) in-between some talks and during breaks was generally feasible, so over the course of the several-day conference you could visit most if not all of them.

Below I will provide a non-exhaustive list of talks I attended with corresponding notes. I didn't write notes for all of the talks and keynotes I attended, so this list is partial, yet still mostly complete.

October 7th

Triaging CVEs for the Linux Kernel - Christoph Steiger & Negar Masoudifar, Siemens AG

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/79/triaging-cves-for-the-linux-kernel.pdf

  • rising number of cves in 2026 (in part due to agentic explosion)
  • on average every bug once per 7 days in 2026
  • updates not always possible (espesially in embedded with various ctrict certifications)
  • maintaining your own kernel fork is too much effort, many companies tried it, many abandoned the idea
  • LTS is the way to go for the most part
  • presented tool: kernel-cve-triage
  • check CVE commit and fixing commit in version history
  • find affected config opts with kmax

If you’re not building the file and you never build it – it doesn’t affect you – around 5-10% functionality of the kernel may actually be used in the build (personal note: similar to how our usage of brain capabilities is limited compared to its potential).

  • kmax helps determing from a file which config options we need to set
  • the presented tool takes 1-2 secs per CVE, mostly due to expensive git history lookups
  • next: comparison with yocto CVE check
  • yocto starting point: CVE -> check whether version is affected or not -> build the kernel, extract include files from debuginfo during building, check if affected files are built
  • minor difference: yocto needs to build the kernel to extract info, while the presented tool just needs the source tree to determine the affected files and configs, no need for building empirical comparison or same kernel version and same config:
  • patched and unpatched classification: tools are similar
  • main difference: ignored category
  • reasons: file determination can fail
  • kmax sometimes fails to determine the relevant config

Shown approaches filter around 80 percent of CVEs, likely it’s the ceiling possible. Auhors suggest adding affected Kconfig in vulnerability reports (kernel CVEs), use LTS and SLTS (Super LTS), join communities like CIP.

Relevant links:

https://cip-project.org/

https://gitlab.com/cip-project

Reproducible Embedded Linux Testing From Laptop To CI To Scale - Anders Roxell, Linaro

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/32/Reproducible%20embedded%20linux%20testing.pdf

ARM CCA on QEMU * OP-TEE on QEMU and RPI 4

  • OP-TEE and CCA are not one project
  • OP-TEE: TF-A, OP-TEE, u-boot, linux …
  • CCA: TF-A, TF-RMM, EDK2, Linux/kvm, qemu, guest/rootfs

Then there is FVP (ARM virtualization platform)

Overall: tuxmake (linux( tuxfirmware (tf-a, op-tee, userspace) tuxuboot (u-boot) shrinkwrap (CCA) → artifacts → tuxrun (qemu, fvp, board)

https://github.com/kernelci/tuxmake

local: python command, local/url files, build/test locally: cloud: yaml…

Overall I felt like the talk didn't really get its point across (at least to me) and was a bit confusing with its pacing. It ended 20 mins before schedule with no questions so maybe it's not just me who was a bit bamboozled :)

Keynote: Open Source at a Crossroads: Geopolitics, Sovereignty, and the Fight to Stay Open - Nithya Ruff, Chair, Linux Foundation Board & Johan Linaker, Senior Researcher, RISE Research Institutes of Sweden & Adjunct Assistant Professor, Lund University

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2Rb7E/keynote-open-source-at-a-crossroads-geopolitics-sovereignty-and-the-fight-to-stay-open-nithya-ruff-chair-linux-foundation-board-johan-linaker-senior-researcher-rise-research-institutes-of-sweden-adjunct-assistant-professor-lund-university

Central point: open source enables govs to collaborate even with rivalry present; industry learned the lesson: open source their own code, co-invest in shared projects and solve problems. Should govs do the same?

In the end there was a list of sovereign AI projects by country (not exhaustive of course): Teuken, llm-jp, openeurollm, aperitus, sea-lion.

Personally I think collaboration would of course ease up tensions, but we should account for the fact that some govs may use others' open source advancements for their own malicious goals while not really sharing their own achievents. So there is a bit of a game-theoretic problem here.

What Is Linux Doing With My RAM? - Vlastimil Babka, SUSE Labs

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/1e/vbabka-linux-memory.pdf

Off the Laptop, Into Production: An Open Source Stack for AI Agents on Kubernetes - Brian Hammons & Nirmal Mehta, Amazon Web Services

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/b0/OSS%202026%20-%20open%20source%20stack%20for%20ai%20agents%20on%20k8s.pdf

Topic: how to run at scale prod agents

The presenters distinguish between outer/inner loop and related tooling

Outer: infra (shared): k8s, VPC, Karpenter, ArgoCD, ACK (AWS Controllers for Kubernetes)

outer (how you operate): build: gitlab /ci/cd/registry

deploy/dispatch: argo for gitops, karpenter for autoscale observability/evaluation: langfuse memory: milvus for vector db

inner loop: agent lifecycle loop request sandbox -> network policy -> identity bound -> harness config -> pod executes -> observe&store -> shutdown/pause/restart

projects for :1) agent orchestrator 2) inference gateway, 3) memory&context 4) sandbox 5) identity 6) network policy

Making the Kernel Chat: How To Get Debug Output - Richard Weinberger, sigma star gmbh

Interesting parallel talk that I would have liked to attend as well:

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/85/kernel-output-debugging.pdf

A Surprisingly Hard Question: How Much Memory Does My System Use? - Richard Weinberger, sigma star gmbh

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/5a/linux-ramusage_oss2026.pdf

This talk was a little bit more practical/workshop-ish with various tools and commands presented to learn about Linux memory usage (which is a huge topic). No, seriously, it's HUGE:

https://nostarch.com/linux-memory-manager

What you definitely need to remember though is the difference between SLAB, SLOB and SLUB :p

Also useful-to-know about

https://docs.kernel.org/mm/damon/index.html

There was a related talk (I didn't attend):

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/67/damon_howto.pdf

Kata at Scale: The Hidden Cost of Running VMs Behind Every Container - Kavitha Daula & Nigel Douglas, Edera

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2RaXe/kata-at-scale-the-hidden-cost-of-running-vms-behind-every-container-kavitha-daula-nigel-douglas-edera

Edera is supposedly an alternative to Kata as a full-fledged platform. The presenters describe their experience and troubles with kata containers. Specifically, kata adds lots of complexity due to its architecture compared to “just containers" (true enough). You now have to manage a ton of stuff regarding the guest kernel – it’s part of the workload. Performance, modules, CVEs, etc. That is, the kernel is no longer infrastructure, it’s production artifact. If you add confidential containers (note: e.g. CoCo, EdgelessSystems Contrast, etc) to that, it becomes even more complex.

Some personal note: while the listed problems are true, I don't think they're necessarily a strong enough argument against Kata - I mean, everything today is so complex, so what's another convoluted project to manage, right? Although I can actually add even more examples that make Kata harder to use - for instance, while with "just containers" like Docker, Podman, cri-o, etc we have a rather established software stack for monitoring, tracing, observability of containers, we don't really have that with Kata, and what we do have is very limited compared to the mainstream (same problem exists with plenty of other heterodox approaches to containers, like gVisor, firecracker-containerd and so on, which happened to be one of the central topics of my Bachelor thesis, so I was pretty curious about the talk and shared production experience). In other words, in addition to managing Kata, we will also need to (largely manually) do a lot of instrumentation of existing tooling (whether eBPF-based or not) due to the idiosyncracies of Kata's architecture, or write our own tooling from scratch just to reproduce a traditional monitoring/observability/tracing stack with Kata - which is in addition to managing the lifecycle of Kata itself. Still, I feel like Kata and projects building on it, like confidential containers, offer benefits that are just too exciting to be outweighted by the added layers of complexity.

Embracing Service-Oriented Connectivity Across OpenStack and Kubernetes - Mitsuhiro Tanino & Rei Shimizu, LY Corporation

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/23/OSS_EU2026_Embracing_Service-Oriented_Connectivity.pdf

Presenters give on overview of their Flava Openstack-based cloud platform

athenz = authN + authZ

https://github.com/AthenZ/athenz

configuration repository

https://github.com/line/centraldogma

Microservice framework

https://armeria.dev

They further describe their custom Service Connect implementation with plenty of detail

In their view, fewer boots is better than having hidden failures in half-working VMs (regarding their NOVA-based solution based on Openstack)

Life Finds a Way, Sandboxed Agents, Observable Verdicts - Henrik Rexed, Dynatrace

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2RaYc/life-finds-a-way-sandboxed-agents-observable-verdicts-henrik-rexed-dynatrace

Setting the stage: intro to some CVEs related to deepseek and flowise; another 2 CVEs related to lack of authentication (regarding ryflow and 9r) k8s agentsandbox operator – scale and isolate agents in the cluster

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox

Available runtimeclasses: gvisor, kata, firecracker, runc (default) Demo with openclaw, tetragon, other tools

Results: runc host syscalls: 6000 in 30 mins gVisor: 996

Sandlock: Rootless and Containerless Confinement for AI Agents - Cong Wang, Multikernel Technologies

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/39/sandlock-oss-eu.pdf

Problem statement: agents do many commands which need various permissions

sandlock wraps every command with its containment mechanism sandlock: rootless, containerless, cgroup-less, based on landlock + seccomp-bpf + seccomp user notifications

https://github.com/multikernel/sandlock

*October 8th

When the Kernel Writes Its Own Code: Debugging Runtime-Generated Instructions - Alexis Lothoré, Bootlin

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/e9/lothore-ebpf-debugging.pdf

Talk on debugging the kernel with gdb (note: interesting to know why pwndbg or GEF were not considered as alternatives to fine-tuning vanilla gdb) Useful tool:

https://github.com/arighi/virtme-ng

primer on KASAN, shadow memory memory granule (8 bytes) and corresponding shadow memory: 1:1 mapping then an example of custom gdb function to investigate shadow memory related to memory region Misc: gdb TUI! (C-x-C-a, TUI view is customizable, C-x s enters single-key mode)

problem: runtime-generated code by example of eBPF programs. Also: increasingly good eBPF support in GCC See e.g.:

https://lwn.net/Articles/1071973/

Side note: Bootlin has excellent training slides available for other topics that I highly recommend to check out

https://bootlin.com/training/

Own Your Stack: Sovereign Kubernetes From Bare Metal To Fleet - Sunnatillo Samadov, Ericsson & Bharath N R, Mirantis Inc.

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/16/Own%20Your%20Stack%20Sovereign%20Kubernetes%20from%20Bare%20Metal%20to%20Fleet%20-%20Bharath%2C%20Sunnatillo.pdf

Sovereign AI infra: motivation Challenges: server provisioning, cluster lifecycle (manage them without cloud API), fleet consistency, drift, no lock-in (modular open-source) k8s: GPU allocation with DRA (dynamic resource allocation)

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-driver-nvidia-gpu

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/dra-example-driver

https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/09/01/kubernetes-v1-34-dra-updates/

Suggested stack: k0rdent, cluster API, metal3 + baremetal GPU servers and AI workloads

k0rdent has components like cluster manager (built on cluster api, flux, k0smotron), state manager (project sveltos as a base); k0rdent observability and finops (based on opentelemetry, victoriametrics, opencost)

Primer on baremetalhost kind yaml file with various fields like bootMode: UEFI and so on

tradeoffs of your own stack: hardware operations, no managed services, slower scale-out, planned capacity

Beyond Strace: Syscall Analysis the Wireshark Way - Roland Knall, Wireshark Foundation

Talk on Stratoshark It finally has a website! When I encountered this project it was just in a repo. The site reportedly went live just before the talk :)

https://stratoshark.org/

One thing briefly mentioned during the talk regarding comparison with other tools: strace can do fault injection! I didn't know this:

https://archive.fosdem.org/2017/schedule/event/failing_strace/attachments/slides/1630/export/events/attachments/failing_strace/slides/1630/strace_fosdem2017_ta_slides.pdf

Rsinit – A Tiny Initramfs Toolbox for Embedded Systems - Michael Olbrich, Pengutronix

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/c6/rsinit.pdf

https://github.com/pengutronix/rsinit

LibreCar: Android Auto on Mobile Linux - Petr Hodina, SolderChef

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2Racg/librecar-android-auto-on-mobile-linux-petr-hodina-solderchef

https://gitlab.com/solderchef/libreauto

Some related/mentioned projects:

https://github.com/vectorgrp

https://github.com/f-io

https://github.com/mobile-nixos/mobile-nixos

Using the Linux Tracing Infrastructure and eBPF for Latency Analysis - Jan Altenberg, Open Source Automation Development Lab (OSADL) eG

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/14/OSSEU_2026-Latency_analysis-Altenberg.pdf

Caching in the Storage Path - How To Gain Performance Without Loosing Data - Werner Fischer, Thomas-Krenn.AG

(wanted to attend this talk but in the end went to another one mentioned next)

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/13/OSS-2026-Werner-Fischer-Caching-in-the-Storage-Path-2026-10-08-1600.pdf

*Your Agent Did What? Forensic Observability for Systems That Don’t Leave Obvious Footprints - Adriana Villela, Dynatrace & Kasper Borg Nissen, Dash0 *

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2Rafg/your-agent-did-what-forensic-observability-for-systems-that-dont-leave-obvious-footprints-adriana-villela-dynatrace-kasper-borg-nissen-dash0

Lots of useful projects mentioned, including https://github.com/perses/perses

(waiting for the slides for other links).

Though I have a feeling I should have gone to the previous talk (that track was more technical-ish in terms of details)

October 9th

On this day, the first 4 keynote speakers were fortunate enough to be placed before Linus Torvalds so the congress hall was packed full :) In parallel: another worthwhile talk by a Bootlin guy, would have liked to attend but I like that Bootlin's slides are always super informative

XDP & XSK Support From a Linux Driver Standpoint - Théo Lebrun, Bootlin

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/01/tleb-xdp.pdf

Keynote: Linus Torvalds, Creator of Linux & Git, in Conversation with Dirk Hohndel, Head of Ericsson Software Technology, Ericsson

A comfy talk about all kinds of topics, from pre-Git times and version control systems to (closer to the end) AI, sashiko and vibecoding (surprised that LT is softer on that now, at least for personal exploratory projects). Seeing Linux Torvalds in person for the first time was kinda similar to seeing Richard Stallman many years ago - they both don't really care about publicity and fame, and act fairly humbly. I like that.

A Native API for Linux Systems With Systemd + Varlink - Lennart Poettering, Amutable

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2RaXG/a-native-api-for-linux-systems-with-systemd-+-varlink-lennart-poettering-amutable

Lennart Poettering had two presentations in a row, and he surely talks fast. Among other things, he announced a desire to eventually switch to Varlink from D-Bus.

The Little-Known Mechanism for Securely Parameterizing Systemd Services - Lennart Poettering, Amutable

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2RaYB/the-little-known-mechanism-for-securely-parameterizing-systemd-services-lennart-poettering-amutable

Systemd-credentials talk

Keeping Track of Resources in the Kernel - Overview and Pitfalls of Resource Management Mechanisms - Bartosz Golaszewski, Qualcomm

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/0c/OSS%202026%20Prague.pdf

Lots of talking about devices and devres

Workshop: Linux Containers In (Less Than) 100 Lines of Shell - Michael Kerrisk, man7.org Training and Consulting

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/ff/containers-in-100-lines-of-shell--OSS.eu-2026--Kerrisk-man7.org.pdf

Somehow this talk felt very comfy, I guess due to the didactic talent of Michael Kerrisk. Great to see some of the things I know in such a gentle way, while also providing new interesting details that I didn't know about (although he didn't have time to finish all slides despite the session being so long :))

Who Watches the Watcher? Hardening eBPF in Production Security Deployments - Hanshal Mehta, Independent

https://osselceu2026.sched.com/event/2RaiF/who-watches-the-watcher-hardening-ebpf-in-production-security-deployments-hanshal-mehta-independent

I was curious to see a talk by someone also interested in eBPF (in)security shenanigans (I did that a lot during my Bachelor thesis), although this talk ended up being more about some specific vulnerabilities in eBPF-based tools while not going into that much detail about eBPF itself and its (in)security, which is quite a growing (though still relatively niche) field of research both in academia (e.g. securing eBPF verifier or providing alternatives to it) and industry (e.g. studying eBPF-based rootkits in the wild). Still, it was interesting to see some of the issues the presenter found in tools like Tetragon.

A Surprisingly Hard Question: How Much Memory Does My System Use? - Richard Weinberger, sigma star gmbh

https://hosted-files.sched.co/osselceu2026/5a/linux-ramusage_oss2026.pdf

Another practical workshop-ish talk by the presenter with useful insights on troubleshooting memory consumption on Linux.

Well, that was a long post and a good memory. Hopefully, I am going to provide similar posts about future conferences I attend as well (which I certainly would like to do).

item.title: Fuzzing TIPC protocol implementation in Linux with Syzkaller
item.description:
This post describes my first experience fuzzing the Linux kernel with syzkaller, in particular its implementation of a rather obscure protocol, TIPC. It was also a good opportunity to explore the kernel internals in bigger detail. While diving into the specification of the TIPC protocol, I carried out experiments in parallel by bringing up TIPC nodes on a local and a virtual machine to simulate a cluster whose nodes communicate via this protocol.

On each node the tipc utilities allow you to configure and examine node identifier and its hash, cluster identifier, connectivity state, address table, the underlying transport protocol (UDP, Ethernet, or the Infiniband protocol used in HPC clusters), and various other parameters.

The /sys filesystem also exposes information from the TIPC kernel module, for example the symbols used in the kernel’s symbol table. In addition, parts of the Linux kernel source that output protocol information to the pseudo‑filesystem /proc (specifically /proc/net/protocols) can be directly seen in the source[18].

In the kernel’s ring buffer (viewable with dmesg) we can see service messages related to loading the TIPC module via modprobe. Notably, the module starts in single-node mode.

To understand how TIPC nodes exchange messages, it makes sense to capture packets with e.g. Wireshark.

The captured traffic shows Link-State information, node addresses, transport protocols, header and payload sizes, priorities, and other fields defined by the protocol specification. Also, the the Ethertype for TIPC, which is 0x88ca.

To use TIPC in a Linux kernel that will run inside virtual machine images for fuzzing, the kernel must be compiled with the following options:

For syzkaller to function properly, it's also necessary to include CONFIG_KCOV, CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_DWARF4, CONFIG_KASAN, CONFIG_KASAN_INLINE, CONFIG_CONFIGFS_FS, and CONFIG_SECURITYFS in the kernel build. These are the minimum configs required to collect coverage and detect memory safety errors. Also we need CONFIG_TUN and CONFIG_TAP to support virtual TUN/TAP adapters to emulate packets arriving from an external network. It's worth noting that for TIPC, as a cluster communication protocol, it's important to have multiple nodes that communicate realistically within a cluster. This requires either configuring the cluster itself or using TUN/TAP to trick the fuzzer into thinking packets are coming from other nodes externally. I also tried adding other debugging options, in particular CONFIG_NAMESPACES, CONFIG_UTS_NS, CONFIG_IPC_NS, CONFIG_PID_NS, CONFIG_NET_NS, CONFIG_MEMCG, CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS for isolation, CONFIG_KALLSYMS and CONFIG_KALLSYMS_ALL for better detection of enabled system calls and kernel bitness, CONFIG_DEBUG_KMEMLEAK for finding memory leaks using the Kernel Memory Leak Detector, CONFIG_FAULT_INJECTION category configurations and CONFIG_FAIL_* for fault injection testing. It's worth noting that some Linux kernel sanitizers (besides KASAN and UBSAN) are mutually exclusive (for example, KCSAN and KASAN) or depend on the compiler used (for example, KMSAN requires clang instead of gcc). Like tracing methods, sanitizers have static instrumentation points at which they are triggered, allowing experimentation with different sanitizers depending on the type of error we wish to detect. Incidentally, this research was also a good opportunity to explore the Linux kernel's tracing and debugging capabilities using mechanisms such as eBPF and tools such as pwndbg, lttng, and trace-compass to gain a more detailed understanding of the network subsystem, particularly how the kernel processes network packets.

Over the course of my tests I tried various setups: different Linux distributions, Docker, nested virtualization (VMware, VirtualBox), and custom images built with Buildroot. Ultimately I decided to use a Debian-based distro as the base distribution because syzkaller expects a Filesystem Hierarchy Standard-compliant system, which simplifies deployment, and I just happened to complicate things by trying to make it work on Guix :D.

I used Debian images for QEMU for VMs, each booting the custom-built kernel for fuzzing. Initially I stumbled on some issues with SELinux policies and external access to the VM images but resolved them, so that syzkaller managed to launch the VMs automatically via syz-manager.

Below is the .cfg file (placed in the root of syzkaller directory) for fuzzing TIPC:

}

After starting the fuzzing process, the web UI at 127.0.0.1:56741 shows continuously updated information about syzkaller’s activity.

System calls and generated programs appear in the console where syz-manager runs (especially with high verbosity -vv 3 and -debug).

The local web interface displays coverage data for various kernel parts, including the TIPC subsystem.

Coverage reports per source file indicate which lines are fully, partially, or not covered.

Although instrumentation points are inserted after compiler optimizations (so reports are not perfect), they are invaluable for iteratively refining the fuzzer. As coverage grows, syzkaller produces more complex programs and syscall combinations, which we can see in syzkaller's reports.

The UI also shows how often each enabled syscall appears in the generated programs. This helps identify which calls are exercised most frequently and which may need additional attention.

From syzkaller's perspective, a program is a set of system calls, possibly connected by resources passed to each other. The arguments of system calls are filled with random values ​​corresponding to their types. If a kernel error is triggered during fuzzing, syzkaller produces a log and report containing the executed commands, information about the stack state, registers, sanitizer operation, possible use of fault injection methods (if this option was enabled during the Linux kernel build), the likely section of assembly code that triggered the error, and other debugging information. The figures below show one such report for the error general protection fault in tipc_udp_nl_dump_remoteip, obtained during fuzzing.

These reports, as well as bug reproductions, are used to reproduce the bug triggered by the fuzzer and subsequently fix it. When possible, syzkaller can generate a bug reproducer not only in its own programming language, syzlang, but also in C, making its analysis more readable. To expand the fuzzer's coverage of the TIPC protocol, I analyzed the source code of the TIPC implementation in the Linux kernel, identifying the main functions, data types, and header files used. Subsequently I tried to understand how the Linux source code relates to existing syzlang definitions, and tried adding some new system calls. In particular, a number of definitions for netlink were missing, as well as messages that can be received externally in reply. Some operations are not supported at the kernel level for this socket type. The Linux code has different structures for different socket types (netlink, packet, stream). I also found several sections of the TIPC implementation source code in Linux marked as FIXME (meaning they require correction by the kernel developers), which possibly affect the effectiveness of the fuzzer's coverage of this protocol[19]. Incidentally, it also seems that there're some things in the Linux implementation of TIPC that are absent in the protocol specification, for example, pretty much everything related to cryptography. Below are some of the syzkaller definitions, with some added during the analysis.

After adding new definitions, we need to use `make extract` to extract the constants, `make generate`, and `make` to rebuild the binaries with the new definitions. During this process I encountered several difficulties with syz-extract (called via `make extract TARGETOS=linux SOURCEDIR=$KSRC`, where KSRC is the kernel source directory), so I used a "manual" method to inject the new definitions into the fuzzer. During normal operation, the syz-extractor utility generates a .const file containing constants and system calls (marked as __NR_ in accordance with Linux kernel development conventions) extracted from the .txt definitions, and numerical values ​​assigned to them according to a specific rule (for syscalls, it's their numbers, for other constants the numbers are from the kernel source "define"s). I manually wrote new definitions into .const in order to work around problems when using the syz-extract utility.

After adding new definitions and rebuilding the fuzzer, the process can be run again, iteratively adding or removing the necessary system calls and pseudo-system calls available in syzkaller, thus controlling which areas of code will be covered during fuzzing, allowing us to find bugs in specific functionality of Linux kernel subsystems.
